readerTitle: Same sales, five times the profit: the forces that decide who gets paid
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Porter 1979, 2008) + 가상 사례 (휴대폰 액세서리 판매점, 업소용 냉장고 부품 유통사, 금속 부품 공장) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 이익은 얼마나 잘하느냐보다 판매 한 건을 놓고 누가 몫을 가져갈 수 있느냐로 먼저 정해진다.
misconception: 열심히 잘 운영하면 어느 업계에서든 비슷하게 남는다. 성장하는 시장이 곧 돈이 되는 시장이다.

sources.text: Porter, M. E. (1979). How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy. Harvard Business Review.
Porter, M. E. (2008). The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy. Harvard Business Review.
두 사업과 공장 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Porter의 첫 논문은 1979년 HBR에 실린 "How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy"입니다. 게시 전에 연도와 제목을 다시 확인하세요.
3번 카드의 "업계별 평균 수익성 차이가 크다"는 Porter(2008)의 업계별 평균 ROIC 비교에 근거합니다. 구체적 수치는 인용하지 않고 일반적으로만 적었습니다.
가상 수치 계산: 두 사업 모두 매출 $5M. 휴대폰 액세서리 $100당 $3 = 연 $150,000, 냉장고 부품 $100당 $15 = 연 $750,000. 15 ÷ 3 = 5배.
softwareNote의 앱스토어 수수료는 비율을 적지 않고 "a cut of each sale"로만 표현했습니다. 수수료 구조는 스토어와 시기마다 다릅니다.

cards.title: Same sales, very different profits
body: Two businesses each sell $5 million a year. Both owners work long hours. Both run tight, careful operations.
One keeps about 3 cents of every dollar it sells. The other keeps about 15. The gap has surprisingly little to do with the owners.

image.label: Two equal piles of revenue, one leaving a small profit and one a large profit
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 높이의 동전 더미 두 개가 나란히 있고, 각 더미 아래 주인 쪽으로 흘러가는 동전이 왼쪽은 아주 조금, 오른쪽은 훨씬 많음. 나머지 동전은 여러 방향의 손들이 가져감. 실제 로고나 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: Which one keeps more of each dollar?
body: **Business A** sells phone cases and chargers online and from two mall stores.
**Business B** distributes replacement parts for commercial fridges and freezers to restaurants in one region.

options.text: The phone accessory seller. Almost everyone buys these, and demand keeps growing
options.feedback: Huge demand attracts huge numbers of sellers. Big, growing demand tells you the pie is large, not who gets to keep it.

options.text: The fridge parts distributor. Its customers have fewer good options
options.feedback: Right. A restaurant with a dead freezer needs the part today and won't haggle over a few dollars. That shifts power toward the seller.

options.text: About the same. Margins depend mostly on how well each is run
options.feedback: Good management matters, but it works inside limits. Two equally skilled owners can face very different ceilings.

cards.title: Same effort, five times the profit.
body: On $5 million in sales, that's $150,000 a year against $750,000. Porter's research found the same pattern at scale: average profitability differs widely from one industry to the next.

cards.title: The five forces
body: In 1979, Harvard professor Michael Porter argued that five pressures shape how much profit an industry leaves its businesses. The **five forces** are everyone who can push your prices down or your costs up:
list: **Rivals:** competitors fighting for the same customers
**Buyers:** customers who can demand lower prices
**Suppliers:** sellers who can charge you more
**Substitutes:** different ways to do the same job
**New entrants:** newcomers who can join easily
cards.callout: The stronger the forces, the less of each sale you keep.
cards.softwareNote: An app sold through a major app store hands a cut of each sale to the store, a powerful supplier of distribution. A tool built into a team's daily work faces weaker buyers, because switching means retraining everyone.

cards.title: Run the forces on both businesses.
body: Here is each force, accessories first, fridge parts second.
list: **Buyers:** shoppers compare charger prices in seconds. A restaurant with spoiling food just wants the part now.
**Rivals:** thousands of sellers online. Two or three local parts suppliers.
**New entrants:** anyone can import cases. Parts need a deep stock and trusted relationships.
**Substitutes:** cheap generic chargers. A dead freezer can't wait for a cheaper option.
cards.callout: Nearly every force works against the phone seller and in favor of the distributor.

cards.title: A growing market isn't the same as a profitable one.
body: Growth pulls in newcomers. When entry is easy, a booming market fills up fast, and prices fall until most players earn little.
So the useful question isn't how big the pie is. It's how much of it anyone can keep, and who else has a claim on each slice.

image.label: A growing pie with many hands reaching for slices
image.brief: 점점 커지는 파이 세 개가 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 놓여 있고, 파이가 커질수록 사방에서 뻗어오는 손이 늘어남. 각 손에 작은 라벨: "Rivals", "Buyers", "Suppliers", "Substitutes", "New entrants". 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: The forces describe the field, not your fate.
body: The five forces explain the *average* business in an industry. Some firms beat that average by finding a corner where the forces are weaker, like a parts distributor inside crowded wholesale.
Forces also shift. A new technology, rule or rival can change them quickly. And don't fill in five boxes equally. Usually one or two forces decide most of the outcome.

cards.title: Now it's a metal parts factory.
body: You make metal parts and can add one new product line. Both options are expected to bring in similar sales. Which do you choose?

options.text: Standard bolts for two big hardware chains. Large orders, steady volume
options.feedback: The volume is real, but two big buyers can set your price, and imported bolts are everywhere. You may stay busy at thin margins.

options.text: Custom brackets for 40 local machine builders who need certified parts within days
options.feedback: Many small buyers, few rivals who can match the specs and speed, no easy substitute. You'll handle more small orders, but keep more of each.

options.text: Whichever market is forecast to grow faster
options.feedback: Growth helps only if the forces let you keep the gains. Check who else can take a share before trusting the forecast.

cards.title: Before asking how good you are, ask who else gets paid.
body: Rivals, buyers, suppliers, substitutes and new entrants all claim a share of each sale. Effort matters, but it works inside the limits they set.
**Try it today:** rate each force on your business as weak, medium or strong. Circle the one that takes the most from each sale.
